title: Hidden Call-Order Dependencies in Stateful APIs
pattern: Public operations on a single stateful object require a predictable preparation sequence, but the interface exposes later operations before their prerequisites and leaves callers to discover the order at runtime instead of encoding it in type signatures.
why_bad: This design counts on other programmers guessing the undocumented sequence perfectly [411:411]. The compiler cannot enforce the required sequence, so callers can produce avoidable runtime panics, corrupted state, and silent logic errors despite otherwise valid-looking calls [395:395].
detection: Inspect stateful or builder APIs where alternative public call orders panic, corrupt state, or otherwise violate required preconditions [410:410]. Include methods guarded by a boolean flag set by an earlier method on the same struct that panic or return an error when the flag is unset. Confirm that this is a stable API progression suitable for representation in types; a runtime error alone does not prove a defect.
fix: For statically representable progression, use the **Typestate pattern** ("bucket brigade"): make each operation consume the prior state and return a distinct next-state type, exposing only valid operations at each stage so correct sequential execution is enforced at compile time [411:411]. Preserve runtime validation for genuinely dynamic external transitions rather than forcing arbitrary events into a compile-time sequence.
source: *Clean Code* (Martin), Chapter 3 & 14 [410:410, 395:395]; Robert C. Martin, *Clean Code* (2008), Chapter 17, G31 ("Hidden Temporal Coupling"); Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 13.
